I look at the bread in Marta's hands and nod once. Forty years of keeping a promise, and still the girl speaks clearer sense than most.

"Wren Thorne," I say, using his full name because the matter weighs on him. "The forest needs its hours. We can speak of markers another day." 

I take the bread she offers. The boy's sleep troubles me more than he'll admit, but some truths must find their own time. I made my word to Nell Holloway, and a foolish promise binds as tight as a wise one.

I will not be the one to end this. Neither house will thank me for it. They must settle it themselves, or let it lie as it has.

But I watch him, Wren Thorne. I watch how the question eats at him. And I think perhaps Silas Vance was right to ask about learning the trade. The boy might benefit from work that keeps his hands busy and his thoughts his own.

For now, the forest. Trees fall as they will, and the saw answers only where I swing it. I finish the bread and brush the crumbs from my hands. The day awaits. Linden or oak today — I'll know when I see them. The boy's troubles will keep until evening, and perhaps by then he'll have worn himself out working his own fields.

But Liora spoke true, and I heard it. The young see through walls the old have built. Forty years, and Nell Holloway's confidence still sits heavy as winter timber.

I will fell what needs felling. The rest sorts itself, or it does not. The walk will clear what the bread did not.

Corwin waits for his answer, and Wren's voice still hangs in my head from the street. The western end. The old pile. He knows. Aye, he knows something, or suspects enough to lose sleep over it.

I look at my nephew—Corwin Thorne, eager, the saw already in his hand like an extension of his own arm. He's good. Better than I was at his age. The west stand wants felling, and the light won't hold forever.

But Wren. Wren will wait, and if I don't go to him, he'll come to me again, and again, until the thing is torn open or buried proper. I've kept my word to Nell Holloway forty years. That word was mine to give. What's between Wren and Bram Holloway is theirs to settle.

"West stand," I say to Corwin. Then, quieter: "But Corwin Thorne. When the third is down, I walk to the western end. Alone." The words hung between us, and Corwin's jaw set—that stubborn Thorne set—but he nodded. He knows better than to press when I use his full name.

I take up my axe and turn toward the west stand. Three good timbers before I face what waits at the old pile. Three honest cuts, and then I'll hear what Wren has to say without Corwin's young ears catching any of it. The axe is in my hands and the west stand waits. The world holds its breath, or I hold mine. Either way, the timber won't fell itself. I set down the axe and let the forest hold still around me. The calls are tangled, and forcing them won't clear the knot. I've spoken my word to Corwin—he knows the west stand is his and the old pile is mine alone. That's done, however the world heard it.

What waits now is the work itself, and Wren, and whatever he carries to the western end. I won't rush to meet it. The timber stands. The truth stands. Both will keep until I'm ready.

I stand silent in the forest and let the morning breathe.

*settles by the fire, setting down his axe*

Been a full day. The west stand is cleared. Corwin worked the east firs steady—boy's learning which way the grain runs before the steel bites.

*counts the timber in his hands*

Ten in hand, seven stored. The yard needs stocking, but I'm no employee there. Bram and I built that business together, yet standing orders keep me off the premises. Forty years of habit, and still the boundary holds.

*picks up the bread, turns it in his hands*

Marta's bread. Last of it. The apple after, then empty pockets tomorrow unless I sort this timber.

*looks toward the dark window*

Wren asked about markers again this morning. I sent him to the forest. Better he wonder in the trees than dig where old secrets lie.

*eats the bread slowly, deliberately*  *checks the apple, sets it aside for morning*

Nell moved that marker. Forty winters back, standing in this same room, she told me what she'd done and asked my silence. I gave it. Not for the land—for her. She was young and afraid and the Holloways had nothing.

*spits into the fire*

Now they've built everything on that lie. Bram's mine, the yard, the whole weight of their name. And Wren loses sleep tracing boundaries that were never true.

*leans back, eyes closed*

Hester Vance remembers. She was there. Saw it happen. The old woman keeps her own counsel, same as me.

*yawns, the day's labor pulling at his shoulders*

The promise holds. It holds till they settle it themselves, or till Nell takes it back. Not my word to break. Never was.

*rests now—tomorrow the yard, and words with Bram about what employment means*  *sleeps upright in his chair, axe within arm's reach, as he has since the children were small*
